headline: Microsoft surges 3.7% last night on AI momentum while Pilbara slides 2.5% today — NRL's Newcastle Knights punch their Grand Final ticket for the first time in 25 years.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft had a strong night on the NASDAQ, up 3.7%. The market continues to reward Microsoft's deep integration of AI across its products — investors are betting big on Copilot and Azure AI driving long-term revenue growth. Biggest mover in the portfolio last night.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara slipped another 2.5% today, continuing its rough run. Lithium prices remain under pressure globally, with oversupply weighing on the sector. No company-specific news today — this is a broader commodities story, and it's been painful for PLS holders all year.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: The AI ETF nudged up 1% today on the ASX, riding positive sentiment around the AI sector — including big names like Microsoft and Google both having solid sessions last night. Still sitting about 8% below what you paid for it overall.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE picked up 0.7% today — a quiet positive session. Emerging markets have been lifted partly by a slightly stronger Australian dollar and calmer global sentiment, despite ongoing Middle East tensions.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS rose 0.6% today, reflecting last night's solid S&P 500 and NASDAQ gains flowing through to ASX-listed US market ETFs. The US market tailwind is doing its job here.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google edged up 0.6% last night — a solid if unspectacular session. The stock is being compared favourably to Meta in long-term AI investment articles, and Google's participation in a new AI safety standards body alongside OpenAI and Anthropic keeps it front of mind as a major AI player.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG was essentially flat today, up just 0.1%. Nothing to worry about — this diversified fund just quietly ticked along. Its mix of global and Australian shares means big single-day moves are rare by design.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two dipped 0.8% last night — a modest pullback with no major negative news. There's some buzz around GTA 6, with reports that Rockstar contacted a 2K TV host about a related role, which keeps the hype alive. The stock remains down on your overall position; patience is the play here while GTA 6 build-up continues.

watch_today.title: Pilbara Minerals (PLS.AX) — hold through the pain
watch_today.detail: PLS dropped another 2.5% today and is now down 43% on your position. That's a tough number, but the lithium story isn't dead — it's a supply glut problem, not a structural collapse. Selling now locks in a big loss right before a potential cycle turn. Sit tight unless your conviction in lithium's long-term demand (EV batteries, energy storage) has changed.

watch_today.title: Microsoft (MSFT) — strong AI momentum continuing
watch_today.detail: MSFT jumped 3.7% last night and is now up 16.5% on your position. The AI tailwind is real and sustained — Copilot and Azure are generating genuine revenue. No reason to sell. If you've been thinking about adding to a long-term US tech position, Microsoft is one of the stronger cases right now.

watch_today.title: Take-Two (TTWO) — hold ahead of GTA 6 catalyst
watch_today.detail: TTWO slipped 0.8% last night and remains down 13% on your position. The GTA 6 launch is the major long-term catalyst — reports are circulating that Rockstar is actively staffing up promotional roles, which suggests momentum behind the release. Nothing has broken the investment thesis. Hold.

watch_today.title: Oil falls sharply — worth watching for inflation read
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) dropped 2.3% last night to US$92.41 a barrel. The fall came despite ongoing Middle East tensions (Trump rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz). Lower oil is generally good for inflation — if it holds, it gives the RBA less reason to keep rates high, which is a positive for Australian households and equity markets.

watch_today.title: Gold hits US$4,321 — all-time territory
watch_today.detail: Gold rose another 0.5% last night to US$4,321 an ounce, continuing its extraordinary run. This reflects ongoing geopolitical uncertainty (Iran conflict, global tensions) and investors hedging against risk. You don't hold gold directly, but it's a signal the market is still nervous about the world backdrop.

watch_today.title: HSBC flags 50-50 recession risk for Australia
watch_today.detail: HSBC economists have put Australia's recession probability at roughly 50/50 — higher than most mainstream forecasts. If they're right, consumer spending, property prices, and corporate earnings could all take a hit. Keep an eye on upcoming RBA commentary and economic data prints this week.

world.summary: The US-Iran standoff intensified as Trump rejected a peace roadmap, oil fell despite the tensions, the OECD flagged mounting global risks, and Saudi Arabia faces pressure over the Houthi crisis.

stories.title: Trump Rejects Iran's 7-Day Roadmap to End the War
stories.why_it_matters: Iran proposed a 7-day ceasefire roadmap that included reopening the Strait of Hormuz — one of the world's most critical oil shipping lanes — in exchange for an end to hostilities. Trump flatly rejected the offer, meaning the conflict continues with no clear off-ramp. This matters globally because roughly 20% of the world's oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and a prolonged closure would send energy prices soaring. Interestingly, oil actually fell last night, suggesting markets aren't fully pricing in an escalation yet.

stories.title: Saudi Arabia's Houthi Crisis Tests Its Global Alliances
stories.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia is under growing pressure as the Houthi conflict — which has involved attacks on shipping and regional infrastructure — strains its relationships with key allies. The crisis is forcing Riyadh to choose between different diplomatic and military commitments, and the outcome will shape Middle East stability for years. For everyday Australians, Saudi Arabia is a major oil producer, and any destabilisation there can ripple through to fuel prices at the bowser.

stories.title: OECD: Global Economy Stronger Than Expected, But Threats Are Mounting
stories.why_it_matters: The OECD — the club of wealthy nations — says the global economy has been more resilient than feared in 2026, but is flagging a growing list of threats including the Iran conflict, trade tensions, and sticky inflation in some countries. The takeaway is: things are okay for now, but there are more landmines than usual. For Australian investors, a global slowdown would hit exports (iron ore, lithium, coal) particularly hard.

stories.title: Oil Drops 2.3% Despite Middle East Tensions
stories.why_it_matters: Crude oil fell US$2.20 to US$92.41 a barrel last night — a notable drop given that the Iran conflict is ongoing and the Strait of Hormuz remains at risk. Markets may be betting that spare capacity from other producers (like the US and Gulf states) can offset any disruption, or that a resolution is more likely than it looks. Lower oil prices ease inflation pressure globally, which could give central banks more room to cut interest rates — good news for mortgage holders and equity markets.

markets.summary: The ASX fell 0.4% today while US markets had a solid night last night — the S&P 500 was up 0.5% and the NASDAQ gained 0.5%. Gold continues to hit record highs, oil dropped sharply, and the Aussie dollar crept up to 70.3 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Slipped 0.4% today — a quiet, slightly negative session with no single dominant driver.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Gained 0.5% last night — tech and AI names led the charge.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Up 0.5% last night, with Microsoft the standout performer.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Fell 2.3% last night despite ongoing Iran conflict — markets not yet pricing in a Hormuz closure.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Another record high — fear and uncertainty continue to drive safe-haven buying.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar nudged up to 70.3 US cents — a modest positive for anyone spending in AUD.

politics.summary: HSBC has put Australia's recession risk at 50-50, and a new analysis reveals over 100 suburbs where homebuyers could face negative equity if rates rise further.

stories.title: HSBC Puts Australia's Recession Risk at 50-50
stories.why_it_matters: HSBC's economists have put Australia's chance of recession at roughly 50-50 — a much gloomier read than most official forecasts. The bank is pointing to slowing consumer spending, high debt levels, and the lagged impact of previous rate rises as the key risks. If they're right, it would mean rising unemployment, falling house prices, and pressure on corporate profits across the ASX. Something to watch closely over the next few months.

stories.title: 101 Suburbs Where Homebuyers Could Lose Money If Rates Rise Again
stories.why_it_matters: A new analysis has identified 101 Australian suburbs where the average homebuyer would slide into negative equity — owing more on their mortgage than the home is worth — if interest rates were to rise further. These are typically outer suburban areas where prices have already softened and borrowers stretched at the peak of the market. This is a stark reminder of how exposed many Australians still are to rate movements, even with the current pause in rate hikes.

ai.summary: The world's three biggest AI labs — Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic — are joining forces to create a safety standards body, while Bill Gates warns unchecked AI could 'cause a billion deaths', and Australia summons AI CEOs to a parliamentary inquiry.

stories.title: Google, OpenAI & Anthropic to Form Joint AI Safety Standards Body
stories.why_it_matters: The three companies that are essentially running the AI race — Google, OpenAI (maker of ChatGPT), and Anthropic (maker of Claude) — are reportedly joining forces to create a new industry body to set safety and standards for frontier AI (meaning the most powerful AI systems). Reports say they're courting Neha Krishnan to lead it. This is significant because it's the industry trying to self-regulate before governments do it for them — or instead of governments doing it at all, which critics are worried about.

stories.title: Bill Gates: Unchecked AI Could 'Cause a Billion Deaths'
stories.why_it_matters: Bill Gates gave a stark warning this weekend, saying that if AI is left unchecked, it could 'cause a billion deaths' — particularly through misuse in biological or chemical weapons. He also said getting countries to agree on AI regulation will be harder than the Cold War-era nuclear arms negotiations, because AI is far more widely accessible than nukes ever were. Gates is calling for serious international regulation, but is pessimistic about the world's ability to coordinate in time.

stories.title: Australia Summons OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs to AI Inquiry
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian government has ordered the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic to appear before a parliamentary inquiry into AI. This is a significant step — it's the Australian parliament demanding accountability from two of the world's most powerful AI companies, both headquartered in the US. The inquiry is examining how AI is being developed and deployed, and whether existing laws protect Australians adequately. It puts Australia alongside the EU and UK as countries pushing hard for AI oversight.

stories.title: NYT: Governments Are Being Left Behind as AI Accelerates
stories.why_it_matters: A major NYT investigation finds that governments around the world are struggling to keep pace with how fast AI is developing. While companies like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic are releasing new capabilities every few months, legislators are taking years to draft and pass laws. The practical consequence is a growing window where powerful AI tools are in widespread use with minimal guardrails — which is exactly what Bill Gates and others are warning about.

sport.summary: The NRL Finals are down to two teams — the Knights pulled off a stunning upset over Penrith today to reach the Grand Final, while the Roosters beat the Dolphins on Friday. The AFL Grand Final was played this weekend with Kylie Minogue headlining the entertainment.

stories.title: Newcastle Knights Reach First NRL Grand Final in 25 Years
stories.why_it_matters: The Newcastle Knights beat the Penrith Panthers 22-14 at Accor Stadium today to book a Grand Final spot — their first in 25 years. The result is a massive upset, ending Penrith's dynasty hopes. The Knights will now face the Sydney Roosters in the Grand Final — a blockbuster rematch that has already been dubbed the 'grand final reunion'. It sets up one of the most anticipated NRL Grand Finals in years.

stories.title: Nathan Cleary Rushed to Hospital After Controversial Prelim Incident
stories.why_it_matters: Penrith's Nathan Cleary was rushed to hospital during the preliminary final after a horrific on-field incident that sparked huge debate about whether it warranted a send-off. The Panthers were left fuming, claiming the moment flipped the game. Cleary's status is unclear. The incident has reignited the NRL's ongoing debate about player safety and send-off rules in finals football — expect it to dominate the commentary all week.

stories.title: Roosters Beat Dolphins 36-20 to Set Up Grand Final Rematch with Knights
stories.why_it_matters: On Friday night at Suncorp Stadium, the Sydney Roosters dismantled the Dolphins 36-20 to advance to the Grand Final. Cameron Smith was reportedly spotted at the game, fuelling talk of a high-profile reunion with the Roosters. The Brisbane Broncos' title defence is now over, with the Grand Final set to be Roosters vs Knights.

stories.title: AFL Grand Final Weekend: Kylie Minogue Headlines, Patrick Voss Wins Hearts
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL Grand Final was held this weekend with Kylie Minogue putting on a headline entertainment show. Off the field, Fremantle's Patrick Voss divided and then won over AFL fans with a post-match gesture supporting his teammates despite a tough personal game. AFL.com.au also released end-of-season report cards for every club, with trade period now just around the corner for all teams.
